children.description_short: An NPR report citing OPM data said the Education Department's headcount fell from about 4,200 in 2024 to 2,300 in 2026.
children.description_medium: An NPR story carried by KPBS reported that the U.S. Department of Education had roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 and 2,300 in 2026, a decline of about 45%, citing Office of Personnel Management data. The figures were reported during a May 2026 congressional hearing. The source does not give exact dates for either headcount or measure service effects.
children.description_long: An NPR story republished by KPBS on May 14, 2026 reported that the U.S. Department of Education's workforce had fallen from roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 to 2,300 in 2026, citing Office of Personnel Management data. The story described the difference as a roughly 45% reduction. It placed the figures in a House education committee hearing where Education Secretary Linda McMahon defended the administration's approach to shrinking the department and shifting some work. This card separates the staff comparison from distinct interagency agreements and budget proposals that had been bundled in the original record. The article does not give exact dates for the two OPM counts, identify which reductions came through layoffs rather than attrition, or quantify resulting service delays or student outcomes. It supports the approximate headcount comparison and the report date; it does not establish why each position ended or measure the effect on students. May 14 is the article's publication date, not a claim that all reductions happened that day.

children.description_short: Education announced six interagency agreements with Labor, Interior, HHS, and State to change administration of selected federal education programs.
children.description_medium: On November 18, 2025, the Education Department announced six interagency agreements with Labor, Interior, HHS, and State. children.description_long: On November 18, 2025, the U.S. Department of Education announced six interagency agreements with the Departments of Labor, Interior, Health and Human Services, and State. The announcement described the agreements as changing administration of selected federal education programs and assigned partner agencies greater management roles. For the K-12 partnership, it said Labor would manage competitions and provide technical assistance with Education Department oversight. This card isolates that dated announcement from the June 2026 agreements and the separate staffing decline. The release does not substantiate the original record's claim that more than 100 programs were transferred without authorization. It describes interagency program management, and its K-12 section expressly says the arrangement remains under Education Department oversight. The release does not establish repeal of the department, transfer of its statutory policymaking authority, or the proposed FY2027 budget figure. The date is the official announcement date; this record concerns the agreements, not a later outcome measure.

children.title: Education Announces Four New Agreements on Disability Programs and Civil Rights
children.description_short: On June 16, 2026, Education announced four agreements with HHS and DOJ covering disability programs, civil-rights enforcement, and related services.
children.description_medium: On June 16, 2026, the Education Department announced four interagency agreements with HHS and DOJ. The release says HHS will partner on special education and rehabilitative services and DOJ on civil-rights enforcement, student privacy, and training. It says federal civil-rights enforcement will continue without interruption and ED will retain its statutory authority.
children.description_long: On June 16, 2026, the U.S. Department of Education announced four new interagency agreements with the Departments of Health and Human Services and Justice. The release says HHS will partner with Education on special education and rehabilitative services, while DOJ will partner on civil-rights enforcement, student privacy protection, and training and advisory services. The announcement states that federal civil-rights enforcement will continue without interruption and that the Education Department will retain all statutory authorities and functions. This card records the agreement announcement and its stated scope. It does not describe a completed transfer of statutory authority, a loss of all federal business or education support, or measurable effects on students and families. The source says these agreements followed 10 partnerships signed over the prior year; that broader history is not counted here. This entry focuses on the June 16 action rather than combining it with the November 2025 agreements, the staffing comparison, or a proposed FY2027 budget reduction. Later implementation evidence would be needed to quantify operational changes or outcomes.

title: DOJ Found Poor Judgment in Acosta's Epstein Non-Prosecution Agreement
description_short: The Epstein agreement was signed on September 24, 2007; DOJ later found Acosta used poor judgment, but no improper factors or professional misconduct.
description_medium: Jeffrey Epstein's federal non-prosecution agreement was signed on September 24, 2007, as a state-based resolution of the federal investigation. DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility later found that Alexander Acosta exercised poor judgment in choosing that resolution and in failing to ensure victims received notice, but said the decision fell within his discretion and was not based on improper factors. The reviewed report excerpt does not corroborate the original card's separate allegation of direct Trump pressure.
description_long: DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility documents that the federal investigation into Jeffrey Epstein was resolved through a non-prosecution agreement signed on September 24, 2007. The agreement ended the Southern District of Florida's federal investigation and forwent federal prosecution of Epstein, four named co-conspirators, and “any potential co-conspirators”; victims were not informed or consulted before signing. In 2020, OPR concluded that then-U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta exercised poor judgment in resolving the case through the agreement and in failing to ensure that Florida would notify victims about the state plea hearing. OPR also said Acosta acted within his broad discretion, found no improper factors behind the decision, and did not find professional misconduct. This card keeps the documented agreement and review outcome while removing the unsupported assertion that Jeffrey Sloman documented direct political pressure from Donald Trump. The accessed DOJ report excerpt does not independently establish that Trump intervened, nor does it establish the opposite; that question remains outside this supported copy. The date follows the agreement's signing, not Epstein's June 2008 state-court plea.
organization_tags: U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida

title: Trump's January 19, 2021 Clemency List Included Drug-Conviction Commutations
description_short: DOJ's January 19, 2021 commutations roster includes recipients with federal cocaine and methamphetamine convictions.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted commutations to multiple people whose convictions involved federal drug offenses. The Justice Department's archived commutations roster lists recipients by clemency date and identifies offenses, including cocaine-distribution conspiracy and methamphetamine-manufacture conspiracy. The roster does not report petition histories, lobbying, payments, or a rationale for each grant.
description_long: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted clemency to a group of recipients whose DOJ roster entries include federal drug convictions. The archived Office of the Pardon Attorney commutations list places recipients under that date and identifies their districts, sentences, and offenses. For example, the list records David Morris Barren's cocaine-distribution conspiracy conviction and Kristina Kay Bohnenkamp's methamphetamine-manufacture conspiracy conviction. This narrower account preserves the documented drug-related clemency activity from the original card without asserting that recipients had never submitted petitions or that money secured their grants. The DOJ roster does not publish recipient-level petition histories or identify paid intermediaries. Legal commentary and contemporaneous reporting reviewed for this repair describe petition bypasses and paid clemency lobbying in other cases, but the material accessed does not connect payments to these named recipients or show an exchange for clemency. No count beyond the two examples is claimed here, and the entry does not attribute a motive to Trump. The original card's broader allegations are excluded.

title: Federal Court Blocks Trump's Order Targeting the Minority Business Agency
description_short: EO 14238 directed MBDA to sharply reduce functions; a federal court later preliminarily enjoined implementation after staff and grant actions.
description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14238 on March 14, 2025, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions and reduce statutory operations and staffing to the legal minimum. The Rhode Island federal court later recorded that most MBDA staff were placed on leave and grants appeared terminated, then granted a preliminary injunction. This account corrects the February date and does not claim all federal minority-business support ended.
description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14238, which directed the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate its nonstatutory components and functions to the maximum extent consistent with law and to reduce statutory functions and staffing to the minimum required by law. The Federal Register text also directed agency heads to report compliance and allowed inconsistent funding requests to be rejected subject to applicable law. The U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island later described MBDA's response: the agency placed all but five employees on paid administrative leave shortly after the order, and the court said it appeared to have terminated existing grant awards in furtherance of the order. The court granted a preliminary injunction against implementing the order as to MBDA; the ruling was preliminary, not a final merits judgment. This narrower entry corrects the frozen record's February date and its claim that all federal minority-business assistance ended. It records the executive directive and documented implementation, not a complete shutdown of every program or the final state of the agency after the injunction. Later agency operations and the injunction's effects are not measured here.

impact_proposal.rationale: The court record describes a major staff reduction and apparent termination of MBDA grant awards, actions affecting a national agency that supports minority-owned businesses. The preliminary injunction shows the order's implementation faced a serious legal challenge, but it was not a final merits judgment; no personal benefit is documented. Persistence is moderated because the injunction interrupted implementation and later operations are outside the evidence assembled.
